faq.q1: What is the Bunny Escape challenge?
faq.a1: It is a playful hand coordination challenge. Copy the bunny and finger-gun poses at the same time, switching which side each picture appears on as the pace speeds up.
faq.q2: How does the timer score work?
faq.a2: It records elapsed time until you tap STOP. You decide when you make a mistake; the page does not track or judge your hand movements.
faq.q3: Do I need to record myself?
faq.a3: No. Recording is optional. If you opt in, the browser records your camera view and the challenge cue without audio. It is not uploaded to FreeBrain; you can preview, download, or discard it after STOP.
faq.q4: Is this a medical or movement assessment?
faq.a4: No. It is a playful coordination activity, not a medical test, diagnosis, treatment, or assessment of brain health.

movements.whatIsTitle: What Are Movement Exercises for Neurological Conditions?
movements.whatIsBody: Movement exercises are structured physical activities designed to improve mobility, balance, coordination, and quality of life for people living with neurological conditions like Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, stroke recovery, epilepsy, cerebral palsy, and more. Unlike generic fitness routines, neurological movement exercises are adapted to your mobility level — seated, assisted standing, or independent — and target specific symptoms such as freezing of gait, tremor, postural instability, and motor dysfunction. FreeBrain's movement library provides free, guided video exercises you can follow at home, with durations from 1 to 15 minutes, tailored to your condition and ability. Whether you are managing Parkinson's disease, recovering from a stroke, living with multiple sclerosis, or navigating any neurological condition, consistent daily movement is one of the most effective tools for maintaining independence, improving daily function, and enhancing overall well-being. Our exercises require no equipment and can be performed in any setting — at home, in a care facility, or during rehabilitation.
movements.howToTitle: How to Use the Movement Library
movements.howToStep1: Select your neurological condition from the dropdown — from Parkinson's to MS, stroke recovery, and 15+ conditions.
movements.howToStep2: Choose your mobility level — seated, standing with support, or independent standing — and set your preferred session time with the slider.
movements.howToStep3: Click 'Find my movement' to see personalized exercise videos. Watch, follow along, and repeat daily for best results.
movements.researchTitle: The Science Behind Movement for Neurological Health
movements.researchBody: Research shows that targeted movement exercises improve neuroplasticity, motor function, and quality of life for people with Parkinson's disease, multiple sclerosis, stroke recovery, epilepsy, and other neurological conditions. Studies demonstrate that rhythmic movement, dual-task training, and dance therapy enhance gait, balance, and cognitive-motor coordination. Regular movement practice increases dopamine production, reduces inflammation, and promotes the formation of new neural pathways. FreeBrain translates this research into free, accessible, guided movement videos you can follow at home — from 1-minute quick sessions to 15-minute comprehensive routines. Whether you have Parkinson's, MS, cerebral palsy, or any neurological condition, consistent daily movement is one of the most effective tools for maintaining independence and improving daily function.

movements.howMovementHelpsBody: Movement exercises target specific neurological symptoms through evidence-based techniques. Rhythmic movement cues help overcome freezing of gait in Parkinson's. Dual-task training improves cognitive-motor coordination in MS and stroke recovery. Balance exercises reduce fall risk in postural instability. Stretching and warm-up routines relieve muscle stiffness and improve range of motion. Tango-inspired dance movement enhances gait, balance, and motor control across multiple neurological conditions. FreeBrain's movement library provides free, guided videos for all of these — adapted to your mobility level and available in 1 to 15-minute sessions.

movements.faqTitle: Frequently Asked Questions About Movement Exercises

faq.q1: What are the best movement exercises for neurological conditions?
faq.a1: The best movement exercises for neurological conditions combine rhythmic movement, balance training, and functional mobility. FreeBrain's movement library provides free guided video exercises tailored to your condition and mobility level — from seated to independent standing.
faq.q2: Can exercise help with Parkinson's, MS, and stroke recovery?
faq.a2: Yes. Research shows that targeted movement exercises improve mobility, balance, and quality of life for people with Parkinson's, multiple sclerosis, stroke recovery, and other neurological conditions. Consistent daily practice drives neuroplasticity and functional improvement.
faq.q3: How long should a movement exercise session be?
faq.a3: Even 1-5 minutes of focused movement can be beneficial. FreeBrain's library offers exercises from 1 to 15 minutes, so you can choose a duration that fits your energy and schedule. Consistency matters more than session length.
faq.q4: Are these exercises safe to do at home?
faq.a4: Yes, with proper guidance. FreeBrain's exercises are designed with safety-first principles and adapt to your mobility level. Always consult a healthcare provider before starting a new exercise routine, and stop any movement that causes pain or unsteadiness.
faq.q5: Do I need equipment for these movement exercises?
faq.a5: No equipment is needed. All exercises in FreeBrain's library can be done at home with just your body and a chair or support surface if needed. Some exercises use tango-inspired movement for added engagement.
faq.q6: How often should I do movement exercises?
faq.a6: Daily practice is recommended. Consistency drives neuroplasticity more than intensity, so small daily sessions beat occasional long ones. FreeBrain's library makes it easy to find the right exercise for your available time.
faq.q7: What movement exercises are best for multiple sclerosis?
faq.a7: For multiple sclerosis, the best movement exercises focus on balance training, coordination, and gentle mobility work. FreeBrain's library includes seated and standing exercises that can be adapted to your energy levels and mobility. Start with shorter sessions and gradually increase duration as tolerated.
faq.q8: Can movement exercises help with stroke recovery?
faq.a8: Yes. Movement exercises are a cornerstone of stroke rehabilitation. They help rebuild motor function, improve coordination, and restore independence. FreeBrain's guided video exercises provide structured movement routines you can follow at home between therapy sessions, with options for seated, assisted standing, and independent mobility levels.
faq.q9: What are seated exercises for neurological conditions?
faq.a9: Seated exercises are movement activities performed while sitting in a chair, making them ideal for people with limited mobility or balance concerns. FreeBrain offers seated movement routines including rhythmic warm-ups, dual-task dance, and stretching — all adapted for seated practice and safe for home use.
faq.q10: How do I start a movement routine with a neurological condition?
faq.a10: Start by selecting your condition and mobility level in FreeBrain's movement library. Choose a short session (1-5 minutes) that matches your current ability. Follow along with the guided video, and repeat daily. Gradually increase duration and difficulty as you build confidence and strength. Always consult your healthcare provider before starting.

faq.q1: Is it safe to start movement exercises at home?
faq.a1: FreeBrain plans are built on safety-first principles and adapt to the mobility level you select. Always talk to a healthcare provider before starting a new movement routine.
faq.q2: How does the movement plan adapt to freezing of gait?
faq.a2: The plan pairs a rhythmic warm-up with a dual-task dance component, then finishes with a stretch, so balance and rhythm are practiced in a controlled, guided way.
faq.q3: Can a caregiver do the movement exercises with them?
faq.a3: Yes. The assisted standing options are designed for caregiver-supported practice, and the seated options keep the session safe when balance is limited.
faq.q4: How often should we do the 10-minute routine?
faq.a4: Daily practice is recommended. Consistency drives neuroplasticity more than intensity, so small daily sessions beat occasional long ones.
faq.q5: What if my loved one feels unsteady or has pain during the movement?
faq.a5: Stop the movement and adjust within the selected mobility tier. The plan is a starting point, not a prescription, and your provider can tailor it.
faq.q6: Does dance actually help Parkinson's symptoms?
faq.a6: Rhythmic and dual-task dance movement are studied for gait and motor symptoms. FreeBrain translates that research into guided home routines.
faq.q7: Do we need the FreeBrain app to benefit?
faq.a7: No. The movement plan is free to use on the web. The app adds session logging, reminders, and symptom tracking.
faq.q8: How do we know if the movement plan is working?
faq.a8: Watch how the person moves day to day and track symptoms. FreeBrain's app includes a symptom and compliance report, but it is not medical monitoring.
faq.q9: What are the best exercises for Parkinson's disease?
faq.a9: The best Parkinson's exercises combine rhythmic movement, dual-task training, and stretching. FreeBrain's Movement Plan creates a personalized 10-minute routine tailored to your loved one's mobility level and current symptoms — whether they need seated exercises, assisted standing exercises, or independent standing exercises.
faq.q10: Can exercise slow Parkinson's disease progression?
faq.a10: Research suggests regular movement and exercise may help slow Parkinson's symptom progression and improve quality of life. FreeBrain's personalized movement plans make daily exercise accessible, safe, and consistent for people at any mobility level.
faq.q11: What is dual-task training for Parkinson's?
faq.a11: Dual-task training combines movement with a cognitive challenge — like walking while counting or dancing to music. Research shows dual-task exercises improve gait and balance in Parkinson's patients. FreeBrain's Movement Plan includes a dual-task dance component in every routine.
faq.q12: How does tango help Parkinson's symptoms?
faq.a12: Tango and rhythmic dance movement are studied for improving gait, balance, and motor symptoms in Parkinson's disease. FreeBrain's Movement Plan incorporates tango-inspired movement into personalized daily routines that can be done at home.
faq.q13: What exercises help with freezing of gait in Parkinson's?
faq.a13: Freezing of gait responds well to rhythmic cues, weight shifting, and dual-task training. FreeBrain's Movement Plan includes targeted exercises for freezing of gait, adapted to your loved one's mobility level — seated, assisted standing, or independent.
faq.q14: Is it safe to exercise with Parkinson's at home?
faq.a14: Yes, with proper guidance. FreeBrain's Movement Plan adapts to your loved one's mobility level and includes safety-first principles. Always consult a healthcare provider before starting a new exercise routine, and stop any movement that causes pain or unsteadiness.

lisbonPilot.introTitle: Free tango movement workshops for people with Parkinson's and elderly with cognitive decline
lisbonPilot.introBody: A free pilot for Lisbon care institutions, now through 30 November 2026. Gentle, staff-supervised and adapted to every ability.
lisbonPilot.whyBody: I'm Jean, founder of FreeBrain. I live with dystonia and have managed it with Argentine tango for years, after training in Buenos Aires. I volunteer weekly at Centro de Dia Nossa Senhora (Santa Casa). Most of our Instagram community lives with Parkinson's, and they tell us the hardest part is keeping moving. That is the problem we are working on.
lisbonPilot.offer1: A weekly 45-minute tango movement workshop for motor and cognitive stimulation, led by me and supervised by your staff
lisbonPilot.offer2: Gentle exercises adapted to reduced mobility, with a seated option for everyone
lisbonPilot.offer3: Simple techniques your team can use to activate residents and patients between sessions
lisbonPilot.offer4: An anonymized summary of results at the end of the pilot
lisbonPilot.ask1: A suitable room and at least one qualified staff member present at every session
lisbonPilot.ask2: A 15-minute check-in after each workshop and a short anonymous survey (about 5 minutes)
lisbonPilot.ask3: Consent forms from each participant, and from anyone who is filmed
lisbonPilot.ask4: Confirmation that your institution's liability insurance covers activities on your premises
lisbonPilot.ask5: Optional: permission to share photos and video (with consent) and a short recommendation if you're happy
lisbonPilot.step1: Meet and agree. We review a short agreement together and confirm your insurance details.
lisbonPilot.step2: Weekly sessions. 45 minutes at a day and time that suits your routine, then a quick check-in.
lisbonPilot.step3: Review and leave-behind. We share what we observed and leave you with techniques and early access to the FreeBrain app concept.
lisbonPilot.safetyBody: Movement always carries some risk, so we plan for it. Your staff stay responsible for safety and medical decisions, and I will adapt or stop any activity at any time. Anyone with high fall risk can sit, watch only or sit out. Taking part is voluntary, and filming only happens with written consent. These workshops are a movement activity, not medical treatment, and they don't replace anyone's care.
lisbonPilot.safetyNote: Either side can stop with 7 days' notice. There are no fees of any kind.
lisbonPilot.appBody: FreeBrain is a mobile app concept designed to help caregivers and staff fit short, fun movement breaks into daily routines, with no complex training. It is still early, and your team's feedback will shape it. We intend to offer it to you as a leave-behind after the pilot, with no obligation.
